Cells measure orders credited to the column, not orders that happened. A green cell can mean the row channel created demand the column got the click for. Shading is what a cell actually contributes, not whether it passed a test. Nothing is excluded for being weak: a nearly-white cell is still counted, at a few percent of its measured effect, and the number stops printing only when it is too small to read. Darker means more of the effect survived the credibility discount.

A pair can be well evidenced and still run the other way — more spend at the row against fewer orders credited to the column. That is cannibalisation, and it subtracts: those pairs are counted in every total on this page, at full weight, with a minus sign. They are not shaded in the grid, because a second colour scale competing with the first made the picture harder to read rather than easier — so the grid shows where credit is gained and the totals are net of where it is lost.

Why they have to count. Keeping only the positive half of the evidence was the single largest error in earlier versions of this page. Selection on sign keeps half of any noise and cancels none of it: a shuffled US — spend moved in time so no real effect can survive — produced 636,379 orders of positive-only halo out of nothing. Two large multipliers were then applied to bring that back down, which is why the page once reported 14% of what it measured. Netting the signs centres the noise on zero instead, and the discounting reduces to one honest step.

The one experiment worth running

How this was worked out

Weekly changes, two-week effects, promotions, and what the method cannot do

The problem. Every budget rises and falls together with demand, so a naive comparison of Meta spend against TikTok Shop revenue mostly measures "the business had a good week". Everything here is estimated with all twelve levers in one model — the ten paid budgets plus email and SMS campaign volume — so each effect is what remains once the others are held still. Promotional depth, gift-with-purchase, November/December and two Fourier seasonal terms are also held still.

Promotions never stop, which limits what can be asked. A promotion ran on every single day of this window — not most days, all of them. So there is no unpromoted baseline anywhere in the data, and nothing here can answer what sales would look like without discounting. What does vary is promotional depth, and that is what the model controls for. It matters: weekly changes in promo depth correlate with weekly changes in total ad spend at r = 0.39, so a model that ignored promotions would credit ad channels for discounting.

How the regions are built, and why not as one model. Spend in one market cannot cause an order shipped to another, so nothing here is fitted across markets. Two models are estimated: the US, and the United Kingdom. Everything shown is built from those two by addition — International is the UK ledger, and Total is the US ledger plus the International one. The buttons above still read Total, US and International; the UK is a working part rather than a view.

The reason is not tidiness. A pooled model is underpowered for any channel whose spend does not reach the whole pool, because the orders its spend cannot explain still sit in the outcome and inflate every standard error. Meta showed the cost precisely when Total was still being fitted: its coefficients came out identical to the US ones, but its t-statistics fell from 3.94 to 2.92, and because this page's weight rewards precision that fall alone would have cost it real credit for no reason connected to the strength of the effect. That measurement is why Total is now built by addition, so it is a record of the decision rather than a figure you can still read off the page. Splitting the UK out of International did the same thing again, doubling the international figure. Television showed the other half of the problem: fitted jointly it read higher in Total than in US, and that gap was the shared media calendar rather than any effect crossing the Atlantic.

What is not modelled, and what that costs. International is 83% the United Kingdom by orders. Every other international market was checked individually rather than dismissed on size. Australia and New Zealand have no paid channel large enough to form a lever, so there is nothing to estimate. Ireland, Germany and Mexico have one lever each, which caps them at a handful of measurable pairs on markets averaging 128 orders a week or fewer. “Other” is a dozen countries pooled, so spend in one would be explaining orders in another — the exact thing this split exists to prevent.

Canada was the close call, and it was rejected on evidence. It clears every structural test: 1,229 new orders a week, 107 weeks, eleven usable destinations and three usable levers — and with only three levers its model is better conditioned than the US one, not worse. Fitted, it produces a coherent and familiar result: Meta spend followed by orders credited to Google Search, CRM Email, Organic, Direct and Bing, at t-statistics between 3.5 and 6.1 and credibility above 0.97. Roughly 12,000 orders a year. It was still left out, because it fails the noise test the rest of this page is held to. Shifting Canadian spend in time so that no real relationship can survive, and then running the entire procedure again, 48 times: the median shuffled world invents nothing, but 19% of them invent more than 1,000 orders and the worst invents 11,295 — as much as the real fit found. That is the same kind of permutation test that produces the “existence” weight and q-value for every counted lever elsewhere on this page (see “How much of each effect is real?” above) — Canada was never added to the US or International model as a lever, so it never received its own q-value, but this standalone check answers the same question and gets the same answer a floored channel gets: not distinguishable from chance at this sample size. A market that small cannot tell its own signal from its own noise here, however sensible the answer looks.

So the unmodelled markets’ orders stay in the denominator, where they belong, but they can never gain or lose credit. That is a real downward bias of about 17% of international orders: whatever reallocation happens there is counted as zero rather than as unknown. It is the price of refusing to let spend in one country explain orders in another, and of refusing to count a finding that a coin-flip could have produced.

One exception, stated because it is not obvious. Every lever in the UK model is measured in UK terms except the two CRM levers, which use the programme-wide weekly campaign count rather than the UK count. The reason is instrumentation, not preference: the send table only opens a UK tab in August 2025, so a UK-specific series would be flat zero for the first year of the window and then jump — a break in the reporting, not in the sending — and it records no UK text messages at all, which would make that lever unmeasurable rather than merely weak. The programme-wide count asks a slightly different question of the UK rows: not “what does a UK campaign do” but “when the email and SMS programme sends more, where do UK orders land”. That is answerable with the data that exists, and it is the question the US rows answer too.

Weekly changes, not levels. Spend and results both trend upward over four years, and correlating two rising lines invents a relationship. Everything is estimated on week-to-week changes. Standard errors are Newey-West, which stops repeated weeks being counted as independent evidence.

How much data this rests on. About 104 weeks against 18 parameters in the US model and 14 in the International one (one lever per channel, plus promo depth, gift-with-purchase and two seasonal terms, plus the shared-demand control), which is not a lot. Excluding November and December removes about 22 of those weeks and costs far more than the count suggests, because the holiday weeks contain much of the spend variation the model learns from — which is also why this page defaults to including them and reports the holiday-excluded view as a secondary check rather than the headline (see the seasonality note above). Even on the fuller, holiday-included window, two US channels (YouTube, CRM Email) and one International channel (CRM Email) are floored to zero because their own spend→orders link is not distinguishable from noise at this sample size — not because their effect is judged to be zero, but because there isn’t enough data to tell. That is a power limit rather than a finding, and it is the reason the floor exists: better to report nothing for a channel than a number this little evidence cannot support.

From a weekly rate to a yearly number. Every coefficient describes one more $1,000 a week. The table reports annual orders, and bridging the two means choosing how large a change to price. Pricing the whole budget — down to spending nothing — is beyond anything the data saw and produces impossible answers. So each flow is sized at that channel dropping from its average week to its quietest week in this window: interpolation inside the observed range rather than extrapolation past it. Every total here is consequently a floor, and switching a channel off would move more credit than shown.

Credit moves, it is not created. Orders taken from one channel are handed to another, so the two sides of the ledger are the same sum written twice and the order total is unchanged by the reallocation. The foot of the table recomputes both sides for whichever view is showing and reports any difference, because that identity has been broken once by a channel silently dropping off the table.

Three questions, kept separate. How precisely a lever's own effect is measured, whether it exists at all, and whether it points the right direction. Answering all three with one number was tried and made the results worse, so they are answered independently and only multiplied together at the end (see “Nothing is counted in full and nothing is thrown away” below).

Does it exist, and how sure can we be? Judged against shuffled data rather than a formula. The usual false-discovery correction on standard errors turned out to be far too generous here: tested on data where each spend series had been circularly shifted so no real link could exist, it still declared about six pairs significant per run against the one it promised. Weekly business series share so much seasonal structure that ordinary standard errors understate how easily a coincidence clears the bar.

So each spend series is shifted at random many times, the whole model refitted each time, and the lever's standardised effect recorded. That gives every lever its own null distribution and its own exact p-value — fine enough to distinguish one-in-ten-thousand from one-in-a-hundred, which matters at the strong end where a coarser resolution runs out. Those p-values become q-values across every lever in the region, and one minus the q-value is the lever's existence weight: the share of what you admit at that level expected to be real, shared by every destination that lever reaches.

Nothing is counted in full and nothing is thrown away. An earlier version of this page had a slider — how much proof to demand — that tempered every pair’s credibility by a single adjustable exponent. It has been removed. In its place every lever gets one fixed weight, applied to everything it touches, built from three questions multiplied together: precision (a measurement-noise shrinkage — a wide standard error pulls the estimate toward zero), existence (one minus the same permutation false-discovery-rate q-value the old page used, now applied directly rather than through a tunable knob), and direction (spend regressed on orders as well as orders on spend, continuously scored by how much of the combined evidence points the way causation should run rather than a pass/fail backwards test). The full breakdown, lever by lever, is in “How much of each effect is real?” above.

There is no second multiplier and no adjustable control anywhere on this page any more. Shared demand between markets is a regressor inside the model, so every coefficient arrives already net of it. Earlier designs are worth naming as things this page no longer does: a pass/fail gate, where a single pair crossing a line by a hundredth was worth 43,000 orders; a pair of stacked multipliers that between them reported 14% of what the model measured; and the tempering slider itself, which could be moved to make the headline number larger or smaller without changing which pairs were counted. None of those are here now — the weight is fixed, not a position you choose.

The floor, and why it has to be firm. Multiplying three fractions together can still produce a small-looking-like-evidence number even when none of the three is individually convincing — the same problem the old tempering slider was built to manage, solved differently. So before any of that multiplication happens, a lever has to clear two absolute bars: its own spend has to move its own orders by a distinguishable amount (a forward t-statistic of at least 1.645, roughly a one-sided 90% threshold), and its total effect — own orders plus everywhere its spend spills to — has to be positive. Fail either and the weight is forced to zero rather than diluted by the other two factors into something that still prints a number. That is why two US channels (YouTube, CRM Email) and one International channel (CRM Email) show no credited effect on this page at all: not because they are judged worthless, but because, at this sample size, there isn’t a distinguishable signal to weight.

The backwards test. A real effect cannot work backwards, so each lever is also regressed the other way — orders explaining last week's spend, not spend explaining this week's orders. A genuine causal pair should find nothing going backwards; where it does, that pattern means both series are being driven by something the model has not captured, not that spend is truly following orders. This is no longer a pass/fail gate: it produces the “direction” factor described above, the share of the combined forward-and-reverse evidence that points the way causation should run, so a lever with a weak reverse signal loses some weight rather than all of it, and only a lever whose own forward link cannot clear a basic bar (t < 1.645) is floored to zero outright.

Measured alone, versus measured properly. Every pair is also estimated the naive way — that one spend series against that one result, nothing held still. The detail panel shows both. The gap between them is what a single-channel reading would have wrongly credited to the channel, and it is usually large.

What this still is not. Observational evidence. Holding a channel still in a model is not the same as switching it off. A spillover here can also mean credit moving rather than demand appearing: Meta causes a purchase that arrives via Direct and is recorded as Direct. That matters for deciding where budget goes, but it is not new demand. The only way to settle a specific channel is to withhold it and watch.

Appendix — every calculation, worked through

One pair is followed from the raw weekly rows to the final adjusted cost, with the actual arithmetic at each step. The pair is Meta spend → CRM Email orders, on the default view: all regions, orders, holidays included. Every other cell on the page is produced by the identical procedure.

1. The panel

One row per week per region, built from agg_master.custom_sessions_orders_spend at daily grain and summed to weeks. Weekly rather than daily because ad spend and orders do not land on the same day; weekly rather than monthly because the model needs more observations than it has predictors, and monthly would give about 25 rows against 32 of them. Window: Aug 2024 to Aug 2026, of which 102 weeks survive differencing and lagging.

Six consecutive rows from the middle of the panel.

2. Differencing

Both columns trend upward across the window. Correlating two rising series measures the fact that they rise, not that one moves the other. So every column is converted to its week-on-week change before anything else happens:

Δyt = yt − yt−1

Applied to the rows above — the week of 2024-10-21 becomes $110,413 of extra spend and 105 extra orders:

WeekΔ Meta spendΔ CRM Email orders
2024-10-21$110,413105
2024-10-28$-91,109411
2024-11-04$23,639-75
2024-11-11$524,7576,815
2024-11-18$-70,974-2,529

This also removes, for free, anything constant across the window: brand equity, price architecture, the customer base, the fact that email volume is structurally larger than TikTok's. None of those need measuring, because a constant differences to zero.

The block rule. When holidays are excluded, November and December are cut out, leaving a hole in the calendar. Differencing across that hole would compute an eleven-week change and label it a one-week change. Differences are therefore taken within contiguous runs only, and the first row after any gap is dropped rather than differenced across it. The same rule governs the lag introduced next.

3. Two weeks, counted together

Advertising does not resolve inside a calendar week. A same-week-only model gets two distinct things wrong: it misses effects that arrive late, and it credits spend for purchases it merely pulled forward from the following week. Both are fixed by estimating the cumulative effect across the week of the spend and the week after.

The natural way to write that is a coefficient on this week's spend and another on last week's, with the answer being their sum. But then the quantity of interest has no standard error of its own. So the model is reparametrised to put the sum directly on one term. For each channel j, two regressors are built:

sj,t = Δspendjt     qj,t = Δspendjt−1 − Δspendjt

This is an identity, not an approximation — βΔst + φΔst−1 rearranges to (β+φ)st + φqt. The coefficient on s is therefore the full two-week effect, with its own honest standard error, and the coefficient on q is the second week's share of it. That second coefficient is what the panel reports as “of which week two”; where it is negative, the subtraction has already happened inside the headline figure.

4. The model

For a destination d, one equation is fitted across all 102 weekly changes at once:

Δordersdt = α + ∑j ( βj sj,t + φj qj,t ) + γ1Δpromo deptht + γ2ΔGWPt + γ3ΔNov/Dect + ∑k=1,2(δkΔsin 2πkw/52 + δ'kΔcos 2πkw/52) + εt

Spend is in thousands, which is why every coefficient reads “per $1,000 a week”. 12 channels contribute two terms each, plus 7 controls and an intercept. The two sine/cosine pairs are a Fourier seasonality term — they trace an annual and a half-annual wave, absorbing recurring calendar shape without spending 52 parameters on week dummies.

Solved by ordinary least squares, the closed form minimising squared error:

β̂ = (X'X)−1X'y

where X holds the differenced predictors and y the differenced CRM Email order changes. The spend block of the solution:

The week-two component is -1.84, so the same-week figure alone would have been 4.28 — the second week gives some back, and the headline is already net of it.

5. The standard error

Plain OLS assumes each week is independent evidence. Weeks are not — a good stretch of trading persists, so errors are autocorrelated and treating them as independent overstates certainty. Standard errors are Newey–West (HAC) with a four-week bandwidth, which reweights the covariance matrix by how much neighbouring residuals actually co-move:

V̂HAC = (X'X)−1 [ ∑t et2xtxt' + ∑l=14 wl ∑t etet−l(xtxt−l' + xt−lxt') ] (X'X)−1,   wl = 1 − l/5

Here the naive OLS error is 1.43 and the HAC error is 0.90. From there:

t = 2.440 / 0.895 = 2.73  →  p = 0.00641

And the 90% range printed in the panel is the coefficient plus and minus 1.645 errors:

2.44 ± 1.645 × 0.90 = 0.97 to 3.91

6. Why “measured alone” is bigger

Run the same regression with Meta as the only channel and the coefficient is 9.35 instead of 2.44. The gap is not noise; it is arithmetic. A regression omitting a correlated variable absorbs that variable's effect in proportion to how strongly the two move together:

β̂alone = βMeta + ∑j≠Meta βj × δj

where δj is what you get regressing term j on Meta's spend term — how much of j moves when Meta moves. Every term, including the week-two components:

7. The backwards test

The regression is also run in reverse — orders explaining last week's spend rather than spend explaining this week's orders — asking whether the causal story could equally run backwards. Nothing acts backwards in time, so a strong reverse result means both series are riding something the model has not captured. This test is now run once per lever rather than once per pair, because it feeds a weight shared by every destination that lever reaches, not a per-pair pass/fail: Meta's own forward t-statistic is 7.84 against a reverse t-statistic of 0.62, giving a direction weight of 92.7% — overwhelmingly forward, but not treated as absolute certainty. Section 9 above works through how that combines with precision and existence into the one weight applied to Meta→CRM Email and every other destination Meta reaches.

The two-week model in sections 3–4 above already nets out same-week pull-forward within each pair; the backwards test here is a separate, independent check that the causal direction itself is right, not a restatement of it.

8. From a p-value to an existence weight

At a flat 5% threshold, a page testing this many levers would throw up several apparently-real results from pure noise, so a single p-value is not enough. The usual remedy is a false-discovery correction on the standard errors. That was tried and abandoned: run it on data where every spend series has been circularly shifted, so no real link can exist, and it still declares several levers significant per run.

So the reference distribution is measured instead of derived, per lever rather than per pair — this is the one place the worked example widens from Meta→CRM Email to Meta itself, because a lever’s existence weight is shared by every destination it touches. Each spend series is shifted by a random offset, the whole model refitted, and the lever's standardised effect recorded, thousands of times, giving an exact permutation p-value. Those p-values are turned into q-values across every lever in the region with a Storey false-discovery correction, and existence is one minus that q-value:

wexist = 1 − q   →   Meta (US): q = 0.0200, wexist = 98.0%

The false-discovery correction is what makes existence conservative rather than a raw p-value would be: a lever cannot look more trustworthy just because many other levers were tested alongside it.

9. Precision, direction, and the combined weight

Existence is one of three factors multiplied together, not applied on its own. Precision shrinks the estimate for how noisy it is: a lever whose standard error is large relative to its coefficient is trusted less, continuously rather than through a threshold. Direction asks the causal question directly — spend regressed on orders as well as orders on spend — and reports the share of that combined evidence pointing the way causation should run, spend explaining orders rather than the reverse:

Meta (US): forward t = 7.84, reverse t = 0.62  →  wdirection = 92.7%

All three multiply to one weight per lever, applied to every destination that lever reaches:

combined weight = wprecision × wexist × wdirection
Meta (US): 89.8% × 98.0% × 92.7% = 81.6%

Before any of that multiplication, two absolute bars apply: the lever's own forward t-statistic must clear 1.645, and its total effect must be positive. Fail either and the weight is floored to zero regardless of what the other two factors would have said — see “How much of each effect is real?” above for the full table, and which two US channels and one International channel are floored this way.

That one weight is applied once, at the lever level, to turn Meta's total effect into an annual order budget — not to each pair separately:

annual budget = toto × annualize(pullback) × combined weight
Meta (US): 269,496 orders/year

That budget is then routed across every destination Meta reaches, in proportion to what the raw regression says about each pair, and capped so no single lever can claim more than 20% of any one destination's own order volume — a channel a tenth Meta's size cannot have most of its orders explained by Meta spend, however the coefficients read:

Meta→CRM Email: routing share 24.8% of budget → 66,909 orders (uncapped)
CRM Email's 20% cap: 43,394 orders  →  scaled to 23,441 orders (this is the number on the matrix)

There is no adjustable control here and no separate per-pair discount — one fixed weight per lever feeding one annual budget, routed and capped, replacing an earlier design where each pair carried its own separately tempered share and a slider decided how much proof to demand across all of them at once.

10. What the scatter plot actually shows

A coefficient from a 32-parameter model cannot be plotted directly on two axes. The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem gives the equivalent picture: regress the spend term on everything else and keep the residual; regress the result column on everything else and keep the residual; the simple slope between those two residuals equals the multivariate coefficient exactly.

x̃ = sMeta − fitted(sMeta | all other terms)
ỹ = ΔordersCRM Email − fitted(ΔordersCRM Email | all other terms)
slope(ỹ ∼ x̃) = 2.4403784804  =  β̂Meta = 2.4403784804 ✓

Identical to ten decimal places. The dots are not a simplified illustration of the finding — they are the finding, drawn. Because the reparametrisation put the two-week total on a single regressor, this remains true even though the effect spans two weeks.

11. From a weekly rate to a yearly number

A coefficient says what one more $1,000 a week does. The table at the top of the page reports annual orders. Getting from one to the other is the step where this analysis previously went wrong, so it is worth setting out carefully.

The naive conversion is to multiply the rate by the whole budget:

2.44 × ($880,416 / 1,000) × 52 = 111,707 orders a year   ✗

That silently asks what would happen if Meta spent nothing. Meta’s average week (Total, this data window) is $880,416, and the model only ever watched the budget move inside a much narrower band. Projecting a local slope all the way down to zero is not something the data can support, and it showed on earlier data: applied across every channel, the arithmetic produced negative annual orders for some channels, because the credit it claimed to move exceeded everything attribution had ever given them. An impossible answer is a useful one.

The fix is to price the flows at a change that actually happened. Each channel is taken from its average week down to its quietest week in the window — the 5th percentile of its own nonzero weekly spend, not the literal minimum, so one anomalous zero-spend week cannot set the whole pullback. For Meta (Total) that is a pullback of $396,161 a week rather than the full $880,416:

Meta → CRM Email, unweighted = 2.44 × ($396,161 / 1,000) × 52 = 50,265 orders a year

Every flow in the table is built that way, before the lever's combined weight (sections 8–9) is applied to turn this raw pullback-priced rate into the routed, capped annual figure that actually appears on the page. It is interpolation inside the observed range instead of extrapolation beyond it, which is why no channel comes out impossible any more. The cost is that the numbers are floors: switching a channel off entirely would move considerably more credit than shown, and this analysis cannot say how much. The pullback-sensitivity panel above prices shallower and deeper cuts than this default for comparison.

12. The ledger, and why it has to balance

A channel’s adjusted total is what attribution gave it, less the orders another channel drove into it, plus the orders it drove elsewhere:

A‑Orders = attributed − in + out
Meta (Total): 797,049 + 141,742 out − 85,385 in = 853,406

Only positive spillovers take part. A positive coefficient means one channel earned orders another was credited for — moving them corrects a misplacement, and both halves of the entry are real. A negative coefficient means more spend at one channel goes with fewer orders credited to another, and there nobody was credited for the orders that failed to appear, so there is no counterparty to debit. Booking those as transfers charges a channel for volume it never held. Negative pairs are reported in the matrix and the detail panel and kept out of the ledger.

Note that the labels invert between the arithmetic and the display: what arrives as credit from elsewhere is subtracted, because those orders belong to whoever drove them. The table shows the two figures the way a channel experiences them — orders gained and orders lost — so the row reads left to right.

Summed across all channels, the two sides are the same quantity written twice: every order taken from one destination is an order handed to some source. So

∑channels in = ∑channels out = 314,371  →  total orders unchanged at 2,204,954

That identity is guaranteed by construction, which is exactly why it is worth checking rather than assuming. It broke once: a channel whose own spend fell below a display threshold was dropped from the table while still appearing in other channels’ flows, so orders left one row and arrived nowhere. The balance line at the foot of the table recomputes both sides on every view and reports the difference.

13. Cost, return and value from the adjusted total

Once the order count is settled, the rest is division:

A‑CAC = spend / A‑Orders = $48,242,283 / 853,406 = $56.53
A‑ROAS = adjusted revenue / spend     A‑AOV = adjusted revenue / A‑Orders

Contribution margin is the one measure here that does not come from the first order, because a first order almost never repays its own acquisition cost. It follows the customers instead: each order is valued at the twelve-month revenue and twelve-month contribution of the channel it actually landed in, and the channel's own ad spend is then subtracted.

A‑CM% = (twelve‑month contribution of the adjusted orders − spend) / their twelve‑month revenue
Meta (Total): ($36,836,142 − $48,242,283) / $62,213,019 = -18.3%

The contribution per customer behind that is twelve-month gross profit less the same variable stack used everywhere else on this page: $6.24 of fulfilment per order, 8% of demand, and 15% of revenue on TikTok Shop. For Meta, $55.76 of gross profit becomes $41.49 of contribution on $70.20 of revenue — a unit margin of 59.1% before any ad spend is counted. Orders per customer across the twelve months is inferred from revenue per customer and the channel's own basket size, so the fulfilment component is estimated; the other three rates are exact.

Customer value is applied where each order actually landed. Orders a channel keeps are valued at its own twelve-month gross profit; orders it gains are valued at the gross profit of the destination they were counted in, since that is where they were observed. That is what allows Meta’s blended customer value to exceed its own — $57.87 blended against $55.76 on its own, because the orders it turns out to be driving surface through channels that retain slightly better than Meta's own base (see the customer-value table above).

Limitation. The unit margin before ad spend sits near 59% for every channel, because it is mostly product cost and fulfilment and those barely differ between channels. So the whole spread in A‑CM% comes from acquisition cost against retention rather than from product economics. Genuine channel-level COGS would separate the two; this panel does not carry them.

14. Sizing a holdout

Everything above is statistical. To establish cause you have to turn the channel down and watch. The section on the experiment worth running applies this arithmetic to Television; here is the arithmetic itself, on the worked pair. It inverts the standard two-sample power formula — 80% power at 5% significance needs the effect to be about 2.8 standard errors — to ask how many weeks a holdout would take:

weeks ≥ 2 × ( 2.8σ / effect )2

σ is this pair's own residual noise, the standard deviation of the vertical axis on the scatter: 892 orders a week. At a 20% holdout:

spend withheld = $880,416 × 20% = $176,083/week
expected effect = 2.44 × (176,083 / 1,000) = 430 orders/week
weeks = 2 × (2.8 × 892 / 430)2 = 2 × 34 = 68 weeks

The relationship is quadratic, so doubling the size of the holdout cuts the time required fourfold. Size is the lever, not patience — which is why the Television design above recommends withholding 40% for twelve weeks rather than a quarter of the budget for twenty-nine.

15. What none of this establishes

All of the above is a careful correlation. Holding a channel still inside a model is not the same as switching it off, and no amount of controlling substitutes for an experiment. There is also no natural experiment hiding in this history to fall back on: across the window only YouTube shows meaningful on/off variation, so there is nothing resembling a clean before-and-after for the channels that matter.

Two specific cautions. First, extending the window from one week to two was not a cosmetic choice — it changed which pairs qualify and moved several adjusted costs materially. A result that depends on where the window stops is a result worth treating as provisional. Second, a spillover can mean credit moving rather than demand appearing: Meta causing a purchase that arrives via Direct and is recorded as Direct. That still matters for where budget goes, but it is not new demand, and only a holdout separates the two.

Appendix — the underlying data

Everything the analysis is built on, in readable form. The weekly panel is the actual model input; the monthly view is an aggregation of it for reading. Nothing here is seasonally adjusted — the model controls for seasonality with terms inside the regression rather than by altering the data first, so there is no adjusted variant to show.

Downloads


Channel summary

Spend, attributed new customer orders and revenue by channel, trailing twelve months against the twelve before. CAC and ROAS here are the channel’s own attributed figures — the adjusted versions are further up the page.

Monthly data

The correlation inputs, by calendar month and region.

Promotional calendar

Every day with a promotion running, in total — which is every day in the analysis window, without exception.

The regressions control for promotional depth and gift-with-purchase. They do not use the other fields here, and that is a tested decision rather than an oversight. Adding promotion type, structure, whether a code was required, deal-of-the-day presence, named-event days, how many promotions started in the week, and how far into a run each day sat produced no improvement in the fit and none in precision: adjusted R² moved from 0.783 to 0.787, and average standard errors got slightly worse, because five extra parameters cost more precision than the new information bought. The richer detail is real, but 101 weekly observations cannot resolve it.

One field was removed after this check. “Promo days per week” had been a control, but since a promotion runs continuously it equals seven in every week — a constant, contributing nothing. Dropping it changed no coefficient in this analysis by any amount visible at fifteen decimal places, and the model is one parameter leaner for it.
